one_liner: Header-only C++ output buffer that coalesces small writes into 64 KiB flushes instead of issuing write(2) per call.
what_it_does: fastcpp::io::buffered_writer keeps a fixed heap buffer (64 KiB by default) in front of an abstract sink. fd_sink calls write(2) directly, file_sink calls fwrite, and memory_sink appends to a std::vector<char>. The API is write(ptr, len), write(string_view), write(char), write(std::uint64_t), write(std::int64_t) and flush(), and the destructor flushes. It does not replace FILE* or std::ostream: there is no operator<<, no printf-style formatting, and no floating-point output unless you add io/format.hpp, which formats through {fmt} straight into the writer.
how_it_is_fast: This is ordinary userspace output buffering (write coalescing). Each write is an always-inlined bounds check plus a memcpy into the buffer, and the sink runs once per full buffer, so the benchmark's 20,000 lines take 4 write(2) calls instead of 40,010. Integers are formatted in place with a divide-by-100 two-digit lookup table and a bit_width*1233>>12 digit-count estimate, so no temporary string is built, and writes at least as large as the buffer skip the copy and go straight to the sink. The gain comes from making fewer kernel entries (about 100-112 ns each on the test host, per bench_syscall), not from faster byte handling.
when_to_use: Code that calls write(2) on a raw descriptor once per record (log lines, CSV/TSV rows, protocol or text dumps) and can accept deferred output. This is the case the 67x was measured on.
Text-output loops dominated by integer fields: write(std::uint64_t) formats directly into the buffer instead of going through snprintf or a std::to_string temporary.
Batch or offline tools that produce a lot of output and can call flush() at natural boundaries (end of batch, end of run) instead of per line.

Hosts with KPTI/retpoline mitigations. The repo's bench_syscall notes that these add several hundred nanoseconds to each kernel entry, so each avoided write(2) saves more there than on the benchmark host.
Projects that already use {fmt}: io::format_line_to formats into a 512-byte stack buffer and appends it to the writer, so fmt-formatted lines need no std::string and no per-line syscall.
when_not_to_use: You already write through stdio (fwrite/printf) or std::ofstream. Those buffer by default, and the benchmark never compared against them, so the 67x does not carry over and any remaining gain is unmeasured.

Output that must appear or survive promptly (interactive prompts, progress lines, crash-critical logs). Nothing reaches the descriptor until the buffer fills or flush() runs; there is no line-buffered mode and no fsync.

Code that needs to know a write failed. fd_sink retries short writes but stops silently on the first write(2) that returns 0 or -1 (EINTR, EAGAIN, EPIPE, ENOSPC). file_sink ignores fwrite's return value, and flush() returns void, so data can be lost with no error reported.
Several threads sharing one writer: the class has no locking, and the repo does not document thread safety.

Windows, or production code that needs a tested descriptor path. fd_sink compiles only under __unix__ or __APPLE__, and all three buffered_writer unit tests use memory_sink, so fd_sink and file_sink are exercised only by the benchmarks.

integration.dependencies: none outside the repo for io/buffered_writer.hpp, which includes fastcpp/core/macros.hpp and fastcpp/string/itoa.hpp; io/format.hpp adds {fmt}. The CMake target fastcpp::fastcpp links all ten vendored libraries (simdjson, yyjson, CRoaring, xsimd, etc.), so copying the three headers is lighter.
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 for this header chain (std::bit_width in string/itoa.hpp); the repo sets C++23 and lists gcc 13+, clang 17+ or MSVC 19.35+ and CMake 3.20+
integration.platforms: any for memory_sink and file_sink; fd_sink needs POSIX (__unix__ or __APPLE__). CI builds on Linux (gcc, clang) and macOS (clang); benchmarked only on x86-64 Linux.
integration.thread_safety: not documented; no internal synchronization, so use one writer per thread or lock externally
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — replacing each write(fd, p, n) with writer.write(p, n) on an fd_sink is mechanical, but output is deferred until flush() or destruction and write errors are no longer reported. It does not replace the FILE* or std::ostream interface.

gotchas: A capacity below 21 bytes is undefined behaviour. write(std::uint64_t) and write(std::int64_t) flush and then write up to 20 or 21 characters without checking again, and write(char) does the same with a 0-byte buffer. Nothing asserts a minimum, and the repo's own 1-byte-buffer baseline overruns its heap buffer this way.

The only integer overloads are std::uint64_t and std::int64_t (plus char), so write(42) or write(an unsigned) fails to compile as an ambiguous call. Cast the value as the benchmark does (static_cast<std::uint64_t>(i)). std::size_t is ambiguous too where it is a different type from std::uint64_t, as on macOS.

The writer stores a raw sink pointer and flushes in its destructor, so the sink must outlive the writer. It can be neither copied nor moved (copy is deleted and no move is declared). If the sink throws during that final flush (memory_sink can throw std::bad_alloc), the program terminates.

The constructor calls std::make_unique<char[]>(capacity), which allocates and zero-fills the whole buffer. A 64 KiB writer created per short task therefore pays for an allocation and a 64 KiB memset each time, so keep one long-lived writer.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No siblings catalogued yet. Within its own repo, pair it with io/format.hpp when you want {fmt} formatting without a per-line std::string, and pick file_sink over fd_sink only when output must interleave with existing stdio writes.
verified_claims_summary: Writing 20,000 short 'line N' lines to /dev/null took 2.93 ns per line with a 64 KiB buffered_writer and 196.8 ns per line with the same writer at a 1-byte buffer, which makes about two write(2) calls per line (40,010 in total against 4), a 67x ratio. This was one first-party run (gcc 13.3.0, -O2 -march=native, commit dfa74f2) on a shared 4-core Xeon @ 2.10GHz VM running Linux 6.18 without KPTI or retpoline, and no stdio, iostreams or other real-world writer was measured.
status_note: Private repo (private:developer-source, readable only with access; 0 stars, 13 commits, last push 2026-09-04) whose MIT-licensed writer is three small headers and easy to copy, although all 21 CI runs have failed, at HEAD from unrelated code (the xsimd benchmark build, and a parse_i64 UBSan error that halts test_strings before its buffered_writer tests).
